title: 3D Armor pieces / rigging….ugh
author: dilberry
selftext:
Working on a fairly easy going RPG, and have found that having a catalog of weapons is very easy to model and implement / rig. Same with shields. 

Armor though… good god what am I doing wrong? I was following this process:

Generate references of each armor piece with GPT dot  
Feed to SOL 6.1 high to run through Hunyuan 3D for a clay model  
Test fit and adjust then bind to the appropriate bones in blender  
Add texture  
Apply entire armor set, adjust if needed  
Feed to Claude who imports into Unity  
Claude scales the pieces to fit our rigged model  
All future pieces will following the same scaling calculations for this model or future models…

Once the damn suit of armor fits correctly. I had a hell of a time with clipping, so we did model replacement (ie helmet replaces the head). Then I had gaps in the fitment with just blank space behind, so we filled with what looks like fabric. More gaps, so I manually adjusted the pieces in blender and saved them. Then the animation tests and the whole suit of armor splits apart like it’s held together by bungee cords. 

Right now I have SOL remaking the pieces as 1 solid mesh instead of slices, because apparently that’s what it did the first time (and took hours). Is this the way? Surely I am doing something wrong?

Would really appreciate some helpful advice.. first major roadblock I’ve hit in weeks now. Low poly, overly baggy armor that comfortably slipped over the model was no problem but this form fitted, actual 3D textured armor set split into 6 pieces (helm, shoulders, gloves, chest, legs, boots) is brutal.

comments.author: TheBigQuestion354
comments.body: Current models suck at the kind of work you are trying to push through it. I tried something similar to make my characters more customizable and I am finding that AI doesn't "see" the model like we do which is why it struggles so much. Personally, I decided to skip it and come back to it after either I learn some Blender or new models come out.
